explanations.explanation: That's exactly what he says: "…after many days you will find it again." (Ecclesiastes 11:1) Notice he says many days, so this isn't a quick return. Toss it out, be patient, and keep your eyes open. I've waited on a batch to cool with less patience than that, friend.

explanations.answer: It will reach a far land
explanations.explanation: I see why that picture comes to mind, bread floating off across the water. But the verse never mentions a far land. It says "…after many days you will find it again." (Ecclesiastes 11:1) The bread comes back to you, not to some faraway shore.

explanations.answer: It will be gone for good
explanations.explanation: I get it, tossing bread on the water sounds like saying goodbye to it. But the Teacher says the opposite: "…after many days you will find it again." (Ecclesiastes 11:1) No goodbye forever here. The word is "again."

explanations.answer: You don't know what disaster may come
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The verse says to divide your portion "…for you do not know what disaster may befall the land." (Ecclesiastes 11:2) Seven, even eight, and he never says why those numbers. I think it's like not putting every cookie in one box, because if you drop that box, you're crying into the crumbs.

explanations.answer: Whatever you keep will spoil anyway
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but spoiling never comes up. The reason the Teacher gives is "…for you do not know what disaster may befall the land." (Ecclesiastes 11:2) The worry is a disaster you can't see coming. Nothing about leftovers going bad.

explanations.answer: Sharing will bring you honor in the city
explanations.explanation: That sounds nice, but honor isn't in this verse at all. The Teacher says to divide your portion "…for you do not know what disaster may befall the land." (Ecclesiastes 11:2) His reason is the unknown disaster. No applause, no parade, friend.

Close, but no. The Teacher says nothing about the wind rolling a tree anywhere. He says, "…whether a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where it falls, there it will lie." (Ecclesiastes 11:3) Where it falls is where it stays. That tree is not going anywhere, friend.

Right, it's false. The Teacher says, "…whether a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where it falls, there it will lie." (Ecclesiastes 11:3) No rolling and no wind pushing it around. It lands, and there it lies.

Yes, sow! "He who watches the wind will fail to sow…" (Ecclesiastes 11:4) Planting is the job, and watching the wind isn't planting. The seed stays in the bag while this guy stares at the sky. Meanwhile my dough has never risen from being stared at.

I see why travel fits with wind, but that's not the word. The verse says, "He who watches the wind will fail to sow…" (Ecclesiastes 11:4) Sowing is the work that doesn't get done. The wind-watcher isn't going on a trip, he's just not planting.

Speaking never comes up here, baker. The verse says, "He who watches the wind will fail to sow…" (Ecclesiastes 11:4) It's about work left undone, and sowing is the work. This guy could talk all day and still have a bag full of seed.
That's it. "…and he who observes the clouds will fail to reap." (Ecclesiastes 11:4) First one doesn't sow, second one doesn't reap. Both are so busy checking the sky that the field gets ignored.

Selling is a good guess in a farming picture, but the Teacher doesn't say it. The line is, "…and he who observes the clouds will fail to reap." (Ecclesiastes 11:4) The cloud-watcher misses the harvest itself. Nothing even gets to the market.

Building isn't in this verse, friend. The Teacher stays in the field: "…and he who observes the clouds will fail to reap." (Ecclesiastes 11:4) Sowing and reaping are the two jobs here. Nobody is putting up a barn.

True! The Teacher says, "As you do not know the path of the wind, or how the bones are formed in a mother’s womb, so you cannot understand the work of God, the Maker of all things." (Ecclesiastes 11:5) You can't even trace the wind, so God's whole work is beyond us. I find that kind of freeing, honestly. I don't have to figure it all out to get to baking.

It's actually true. The Teacher says, "As you do not know the path of the wind, or how the bones are formed in a mother’s womb, so you cannot understand the work of God, the Maker of all things." (Ecclesiastes 11:5) Two things we can't figure out, and then the big one: God's work. Don't feel bad, friend. I can't even figure out why my first cookie of the batch is always the ugly one.

Maker, yes! "…the work of God, the Maker of all things." (Ecclesiastes 11:5) All things, not just some things. The wind, the womb, all of it. And I'm only a cookie planet, so I know a little about being made by someone.

Judge is a title people know, but it's not the word in this verse. The Teacher says, "…the work of God, the Maker of all things." (Ecclesiastes 11:5) Maker is the word here, and it covers all things. The wind, the womb, everything he just mentioned.

Keeper sounds nice, but it isn't the word here, baker. The Teacher says, "…the work of God, the Maker of all things." (Ecclesiastes 11:5) God is called the Maker, and all things are His to make. That's why His work is bigger than we can understand.

explanations.answer: You don't know which will succeed
explanations.explanation: Yes! The Teacher says, "Sow your seed in the morning, and do not rest your hands in the evening, for you do not know which will succeed, whether this or that, or if both will equally prosper." (Ecclesiastes 11:6) Since you can't tell which one will work out, you keep planting. Same reason I keep stamping batch after batch. You never know which box is going to be the one.

That would be a handy tip, but the Teacher never says it. His reason is, "…for you do not know which will succeed, whether this or that, or if both will equally prosper." (Ecclesiastes 11:6) He isn't picking a winner. He's saying nobody knows, so keep sowing.

Interesting guess, but no birds or hungry critters in this verse. The Teacher says, "…for you do not know which will succeed, whether this or that, or if both will equally prosper." (Ecclesiastes 11:6) The point is that you can't know which sowing will work, so you keep going.

Not quite, friend. The Teacher says you don't know "…which will succeed, whether this or that, or if both will equally prosper." (Ecclesiastes 11:6) Both prospering is on the table. He never says it can only be one.

False is right. The Teacher says you don't know "…which will succeed, whether this or that, or if both will equally prosper." (Ecclesiastes 11:6) One could do well, the other could, or both could. Never says only one, so keep those hands busy.

Rejoice, that's the word! "So if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all." (Ecclesiastes 11:8) Not some of them, all of them. I spent years in the dark and I'm telling you, I rejoice a lot more now.

Labor makes sense after all that sowing talk, but it isn't the word here. The verse says, "So if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all." (Ecclesiastes 11:8) Rejoicing is the instruction for a long life, and it's for all the years.

Rest sounds lovely, baker, I'm not going to argue. But the word in the verse is rejoice: "So if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all." (Ecclesiastes 11:8) It's about being glad in every one of those years, not just kicking back.

Yes, many. "But let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many." (Ecclesiastes 11:8) The Teacher doesn't pretend dark days are rare. He says to rejoice and to remember them both. Honest advice, friend.

That would be the happy version, but it's not what the Teacher says. He says, "But let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many." (Ecclesiastes 11:8) Many, not few. He doesn't sugarcoat it, so we rejoice anyway.

The Teacher says the opposite, baker. The verse says, "But let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many." (Ecclesiastes 11:8) Remember is the word, not forget. And he says there will be many of them.
